newsitem.title: USA: U.S. base metal premiums stable in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. base metal premiums stable in quiet trade.

text.p: U.S. base metals premiums remain in line with last week's levels as physicial business is steady but fairly quiet, dealers said.
Aluminum premiums have stayed strong, with small amounts for prompt delivery in April at 6.00-6.50 cents per pound over LME cash.
The premiums were 5.25 to 6.00 cents per pound for deliveries between now and the end of May, traders said.
"Once metal prices are 75 cents a lb or under, then people are comfortable with that level, especially consumers with fixed prices purchases," a dealer said.
LME cash closed at the equivalent of 69 cents a pound on Wednesday.

Producers were still not sellers in large quantities - Alcoa and Northwest Aluminum put in bids for government stockpiled metal on Wednesday -- thereby putting extra importance on imported metal which will help to keep premiums from falling too much, traders said.
Aluminum alloy prices have avoided further sharp dips this week and were quoted at 74 to 76 cents a lb for benchmark A380 metal.

One alloy smelter official noted that U.S. car sales fell in March for many of the major assemblers, and a better idea of second quarter alloy demand will be had in about a month's time. Auto manufacturing is a key alloy consumer.

Zinc premiums were also stable at 5.25 to 5.75 cents a lb over LME cash. U.S. Stockpile sold 2,557 tonnes of zinc to five companies on Wednesday at relatively low premiums on some of the awards, merchants said.
Nickel premiums were also steady at 10 to 13 cents per lb over LME cash for melting grade material.

Tin premiums were quoted in a wide range, with some producer sources noting a recovery in low lead premiums to $180 to $200 over LME cash per tonne price or 8.00 to 9.00 cents a lb, while other traders said low-lead premiums were lower.
In the secondary market, copper scrap was said to be tight as dealers hold on to material after the sharp dip in prices in the past two weeks. They were hoping prices will recover.
Some merchants sensed a slight slowdown in business since last month, but stressed that this should be put in perspective with the good demand previously.
"The brass and tube mills are very busy, but there is not a lot of scrap going round...Scrap is tight," a Midwest dealer said.
